parts.title: First contact with a FortiGate you've never seen
tasks: Find the hostname, the serial number and the firmware version.
Find which interface and gateway the default route uses.
Find which firewall policy publishes the appointment portal (citas.clinicasanrafael.co).

ran.fail: Start with `get system status`: it's the first command on any new FortiGate.

ran.cmd: get router info routing-table|get router info rout

answer.hint: It's in the output of `get system status`, the Serial-Number line.
answer.why: Serial numbers go in every PS report and every TAC case.

checks.text: Default route: which interface and gateway? (e.g. port1 192.0.2.1)

answer.hint: Look for the S* line in the routing table.

checks.text: Which policy ID publishes the portal?

answer.hint: `show firewall policy`, look for the policy whose destination is a VIP.
answer.why: Policy 2 (Citas-Publish) allows HTTPS from wan1 to the VIP VIP-CITAS-443.

hints: Three read-only commands answer everything: one for the system, one for routing, one for policies.
`get system status`, `get router info routing-table all`, `show firewall policy`.

solution.FGT-SR:
get system status
get router info routing-table all
show firewall policy

parts.explain:
A PS consultant's first hour on an unknown box is read-only. `get system status` gives model, firmware,
serial, HA mode and VDOM mode; the routing table tells you how traffic leaves; `show firewall policy`
shows what's allowed. Note what you find before you touch anything: it's your baseline and your rollback.

parts.title: show, get and full-configuration
tasks: Find the default admin idle timeout (it isn't in `show system global`, because it's a default).
Rename the FortiGate to FGT-SR-SMR01 (site SR, city code SMR, unit 01).
Set the admin idle timeout to 15 minutes.
Give the dmz interface the alias "DMZ-Portal".

checks.text: What is the default admintimeout, in minutes?

answer.hint: `show full-configuration system global`, then find admintimeout. Or `get system global`.
answer.why: Defaults never appear in plain `show`; that's why reading a config needs full-configuration.

hints: `show` hides defaults. Try `show full-configuration system global` or `get system global`.
`config system global`, then `set hostname ...` and `set admintimeout ...`, then `end`.
Aliases live on the interface: `config system interface`, `edit dmz`, `set alias DMZ-Portal`.

solution.FGT-SR:
show full-configuration system global
config system global
set hostname FGT-SR-SMR01
set admintimeout 15
end
config system interface
edit dmz
set alias DMZ-Portal
next
end

parts.explain:
Changes in an `edit` take effect at `next` or `end`; `abort` throws them away. When you document a
customer's config, use `show` to see their intent and `show full-configuration` when a default matters.
The prompt changes with the hostname immediately: that's how you know `end` committed it.

parts.title: Back up before you touch anything
tasks: Back up the configuration to TFTP 10.10.10.50 before any change (file name of your choice).
Rename WEB-CITAS to SRV-CITAS-WEB and check that policy 3 still works.
Delete OLD-PRINTER.
Try to delete LAN-Staff, read the error, and answer why it failed.

checks.text: Configuration backed up before the first change
SRV-CITAS-WEB exists and policy 3 uses it
Staff can still reach the portal over HTTPS

answer.hint: Read the error: 'The entry is used by other ... entries'.
answer.why: FortiOS won't delete an object a policy references. Rename updates references for you; delete doesn't.

hints: The backup command starts with `execute backup config tftp`, then a file name, then the server IP.
`config firewall address`, then `rename WEB-CITAS to SRV-CITAS-WEB`, then `delete OLD-PRINTER`.

solution.FGT-SR:
execute backup config tftp fgt-sr-before-cleanup.conf 10.10.10.50
config firewall address
rename WEB-CITAS to SRV-CITAS-WEB
delete OLD-PRINTER
delete LAN-Staff
end

parts.explain:
`rename` keeps every reference pointing at the object; delete-and-recreate would break the policies that use it.
FortiOS refuses to delete an object in use ("The entry is used by other N entries"); you'd first remove it from
each policy. And the backup comes first: it's your rollback if the window goes wrong.

parts.title: Read the routing table and the session table
tasks: From RECEPCION, browse to www.fortinet.com (curl https://www.fortinet.com) so a session exists.
On FGT-SR, filter the session list to RECEPCION's IP and read the session.
Find which interface traffic to 172.16.40.15 would use.

ran.fail: Run curl https://www.fortinet.com on RECEPCION first.
Filter first: `diagnose sys session filter src <ip>`, then `diagnose sys session list`.

checks.text: Which policy ID handled RECEPCION's web session?

answer.hint: Look for policy_id= in the session.
answer.why: policy_id=1 (Staff-Internet).

checks.text: Which source IP did the session leave with (after SNAT)?

answer.hint: The act=snat line shows the translated address in brackets.
answer.why: SNAT to wan1's IP, 203.0.113.2.

checks.text: Which interface would traffic to 172.16.40.15 leave through?

answer.hint: `get router info routing-table details 172.16.40.15`.
answer.why: The static route 172.16.40.0/24 via 10.10.10.254 points out internal.

hints: Session list is long on a real box. Always filter: `diagnose sys session filter clear`, then `diagnose sys session filter src <RECEPCION IP>`.
RECEPCION's IP comes from DHCP: run ipconfig there.

solution.FGT-SR:
diagnose sys session filter clear
diagnose sys session filter src 10.10.10.100
diagnose sys session list
get router info routing-table details 172.16.40.15

parts.explain:
The session table is the truth about traffic the FortiGate has already accepted: interfaces, gateway,
NAT and the policy ID. In production it holds thousands of entries, so filter first. `routing-table details <ip>`
answers "where would this go" without sending a packet.

labs.title: Clínica San Rafael: day-one deployment
labs.customer: Clínica San Rafael (40 staff, Santa Marta)
labs.brief:
**SOW 2026-118 · FortiGate-60F deployment.** The clinic replaces a consumer router with a FortiGate-60F.

**In scope:** WAN on Claro (203.0.113.2/28, gateway 203.0.113.1), staff LAN 10.10.10.0/24 with DHCP,
a DMZ for the appointment portal (WEB-CITAS, 192.168.50.10), Internet for staff, publishing the portal
over HTTPS only, and admin hardening.
**Out of scope:** Wi-Fi, VPN, security profiles (phase 2).
**Change window:** tonight 20:00–23:00. **Acceptance:** the checks of each part.

The project has five parts. Each one unlocks when the previous one passes, like the milestones of a real SOW.

parts.title: Interfaces and management access
parts.brief: Address the three interfaces. Management (HTTPS, SSH) only from the staff LAN; the WAN answers ping and nothing else.
tasks: wan1: 203.0.113.2/28, allow ping only, alias Claro.
internal: 10.10.10.1/24, allow ping, HTTPS and SSH, alias LAN-Staff.
dmz: 192.168.50.1/24, allow ping only.

checks.text: No HTTPS, HTTP, SSH or Telnet admin on wan1
The portal server pings its gateway 192.168.50.1
The DMZ can't open the GUI

hints: Everything here is under `config system interface`, one `edit` per port.
allowaccess replaces the whole list: `set allowaccess ping https ssh`.
`edit wan1` / `set ip 203.0.113.2/28` / `set allowaccess ping` / `set alias Claro` / `next`.

solution.FGT-SR:
config system interface
edit wan1
set ip 203.0.113.2/28
set allowaccess ping
set alias Claro
next
edit internal
set ip 10.10.10.1/24
set allowaccess ping https ssh
set alias LAN-Staff
next
edit dmz
set ip 192.168.50.1/24
set allowaccess ping
next
end

parts.explain:
allowaccess controls which management services an interface answers. Exposing HTTPS or SSH on a WAN is the most
common finding in FortiGate health checks; it's also the first thing attackers scan for.

parts.title: DHCP and DNS for staff
parts.brief:
Staff PCs use DHCP. Leases from 10.10.10.100 to 10.10.10.199, gateway 10.10.10.1. The FortiGate uses Google and
Cloudflare as DNS, and hands the same servers to the PCs.
tasks: System DNS: primary 8.8.8.8, secondary 1.1.1.1.
DHCP server on internal: range 10.10.10.100-10.10.10.199, gateway 10.10.10.1, mask 255.255.255.0, DNS = the system DNS.
Renew the lease on RECEPCION (ipconfig /renew) and check it.

checks.text: RECEPCION gets an address in 10.10.10.100-199 with gateway 10.10.10.1

hints: DNS: `config system dns` / `set primary ...` / `set secondary ...` / `end`.
The range is a table inside the DHCP server: `config ip-range` / `edit 1` / `set start-ip ...` / `set end-ip ...` / `next` / `end`.
`set dns-service default` hands out the FortiGate's own system DNS servers.

solution.FGT-SR:
config system dns
set primary 8.8.8.8
set secondary 1.1.1.1
end
config system dhcp server
edit 1
set interface internal
set default-gateway 10.10.10.1
set netmask 255.255.255.0
set dns-service default
config ip-range
edit 1
set start-ip 10.10.10.100
set end-ip 10.10.10.199
next
end
next
end

parts.explain:
dns-service has three modes: default (system DNS), specify (dns-server1/2) and local (the FortiGate itself as a DNS
server). Most "Internet doesn't work" tickets on day one are a DHCP lease without a DNS server.

parts.title: Internet for staff
parts.brief: Staff browse the Internet through Claro. Use an address object for the LAN and source NAT to wan1's IP.
tasks: Default route to 203.0.113.1 through wan1.
Address object LAN-Staff = 10.10.10.0/24.
Policy internal → wan1 for LAN-Staff, NAT enabled, named Staff-Internet.

checks.text: The policy uses the LAN-Staff object, not 'all'

hints: Without a route the FortiGate drops the packet before any policy: check `get router info routing-table all`.
`config router static` / `edit 0` / `set gateway 203.0.113.1` / `set device wan1` / `next` / `end`.
Private 10.x addresses can't come back from the Internet: the policy needs `set nat enable`.

solution.FGT-SR:
config router static
edit 0
set gateway 203.0.113.1
set device wan1
next
end
config firewall address
edit LAN-Staff
set subnet 10.10.10.0/24
next
end
config firewall policy
edit 0
set name Staff-Internet
set srcintf internal
set dstintf wan1
set srcaddr LAN-Staff
set dstaddr all
set action accept
set schedule always
set service ALL
set nat enable
next
end

parts.explain:
FortiOS order for a new session: route lookup first (which also decides the egress interface), then the policy for
that interface pair, then NAT. No route means no policy match is even attempted. Using an address object instead of
'all' documents intent and keeps rogue subnets out.

parts.title: Publish the appointment portal
parts.brief:
Patients book at **https://citas.clinicasanrafael.co** (DNS already points to 203.0.113.2). Publish WEB-CITAS on
wan1's IP, HTTPS only. The portal logs client IPs for audit, so the server must see the patient's real address.
tasks: VIP VIP-CITAS-443: 203.0.113.2:443 on wan1 → 192.168.50.10:443 (port forwarding).
Policy wan1 → dmz to the VIP, service HTTPS only, no NAT.
Test from HOME-PC: curl https://citas.clinicasanrafael.co

checks.text: A patient (HOME-PC) reaches the portal over HTTPS
WEB-CITAS sees the patient's real IP (100.25.7.9)
SSH to the portal is not exposed

hints: A VIP is just the translation. Nothing passes until a policy uses the VIP as destination.
`config firewall vip` / `edit VIP-CITAS-443` / `set extip 203.0.113.2` / `set mappedip 192.168.50.10` / `set extintf wan1` / `set portforward enable` / `set extport 443` / `set mappedport 443`.
In the policy, `set dstaddr VIP-CITAS-443` and `set service HTTPS`; leave NAT disabled so the server sees real client IPs.

solution.FGT-SR:
config firewall vip
edit VIP-CITAS-443
set extip 203.0.113.2
set mappedip 192.168.50.10
set extintf wan1
set portforward enable
set extport 443
set mappedport 443
next
end
config firewall policy
edit 0
set name Citas-Publish
set srcintf wan1
set dstintf dmz
set srcaddr all
set dstaddr VIP-CITAS-443
set action accept
set schedule always
set service HTTPS
next
end

parts.explain:
With port forwarding the VIP translates only TCP 443, so 22 and 80 still go to the FortiGate itself (and are dropped,
because wan1 allows only ping). Enabling NAT on an inbound policy would hide every patient behind the DMZ interface IP
and break the portal's audit log: a classic day-two complaint.

parts.title: Hand-over hardening
parts.brief:
Before hand-over, the clinic's security officer wants admin logins limited to the staff LAN, a 10-minute idle timeout,
and the final config saved to the NAS.
tasks: Trusted host for the admin account: 10.10.10.0/24.
Admin idle timeout: 10 minutes.
Back up the configuration to TFTP 10.10.10.50.

checks.text: admin can only log in from 10.10.10.0/24

hints: Trusted hosts are per admin: `config system admin` / `edit admin` / `set trusthost1 10.10.10.0/24`.
Backup: `execute backup config tftp <file> 10.10.10.50`.

solution.FGT-SR:
config system admin
edit admin
set trusthost1 10.10.10.0/24
next
end
config system global
set admintimeout 10
end
execute backup config tftp fgt-sr-handover.conf 10.10.10.50

parts.explain:
Trusted hosts are checked on top of allowaccess: an address outside them can't log in even where HTTPS is allowed.
Configure them on every admin account, or the one you forget becomes the way in. The final backup goes into the
hand-over pack with the as-built document.
